title: The kitchen friar (Brother Lawrence, 17th century)
hook: a Carmelite lay brother who found God among the pots and pans

segments.voice: Yesterday, hesychasm: a prayer said with every breath. Today, a man who prayed over a frying pan.

A friary kitchen in Paris, in the 1600s. Steam, noise, pots on the boil, people wanting bread and soup at once. In the middle of it, a big, clumsy man with a bad leg, an old soldier, who by his own account had a natural dislike of kitchen work. He wasn't a priest. He never wrote a book. He was a lay brother, which meant he did the chores. And yet a priest came to talk with him about prayer, then went away and wrote the conversations down.
screen: `A LOUD KITCHEN IN PARIS.` → `AN OLD SOLDIER WHO HATED COOKING.` → `A PRIEST WRITES DOWN HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: His name was Nicholas Herman; in the Carmelite order he became Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. First, how it began. As a young man, before he joined, he looked at a bare tree in winter, no leaves, no fruit, and it struck him that in a few months it would be green and heavy with fruit again. He said that moment gave him a sense of God's care that never left him. A tree in winter. That's all it took. Second, the kitchen. He was put to work cooking, which he disliked, so he made a choice: he would do every small task for the love of God. Turning a cake in the pan, picking a straw up off the floor: each could be a way of loving God. Nothing had to be grand. Third, the method, if you can call it that. He called it the practice of the presence of God: talking to God simply, all day, in the middle of whatever he was doing, not waiting for chapel. He said the time of work and the time of prayer were no different for him; in the noise of the kitchen he felt as calm as if he were kneeling before the Blessed Sacrament. Fourth, how we know. He wrote very little. After he died, that priest gathered the conversations and a handful of letters into a small book, The Practice of the Presence of God. It's short enough to read in an evening, small enough for a coat pocket.
screen: `A BARE TREE IN WINTER.` · `EVERY SMALL TASK FOR LOVE.` · `THE PRACTICE OF THE PRESENCE.` · `A SMALL BOOK, GATHERED AFTER.` · then, large: `THE TIME OF WORK IS THE TIME OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: If there's a sink nearby, wash one plate at a time in warm water; if not, picture it, and don't rush to be done. If you pray, talk to God the way Brother Lawrence did, plainly, as if God were standing at the counter beside you. If you don't, give the plate your whole attention, and let that be enough.
Brother Lawrence. A Carmelite lay brother in seventeenth-century Paris who practiced God's presence among the pots and pans of the friary kitchen. Today's word.
Your line: god among the pots. No task is too small to be done for love. That's day two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics and other Christians who read Brother Lawrence's The Practice of the Presence of God try to keep a simple, running conversation with God through ordinary work, especially housework and repetitive tasks.

notes: Brother Lawrence (Nicolas Herman, c. 1614–1691), Discalced Carmelite lay brother in Paris; former soldier with a leg injury; later also worked mending sandals. Confirm details.

The bare-tree conversion at about age 18, his stated aversion to kitchen work, turning the cake in the pan, and the comparison of the noisy kitchen to kneeling before the Blessed Sacrament are paraphrased from the Conversations; no English translation is quoted. Confirm the paraphrases.
Compiled by Abbé Joseph de Beaufort; first published around 1692–1694. Confirm date.
